items.title: 95% confidence interval
items.prompt: A sample of n = 64 has mean x̄ = 52.3. The population standard deviation is known: σ = 8. Build a 95% confidence interval for the population mean μ, and say in one sentence what it means.
items.hint: Standard error first: σ/√n. The 95% z multiplier is 1.96.
items.answer:
SE = σ/√n = 8/√64 = 8/8 = 1.
Margin = 1.96 × 1 = 1.96.
CI = 52.3 ± 1.96 = (50.34, 54.26).
Meaning: the procedure captures μ in 95% of repeated samples. It is not a 95% probability that μ lies in this particular interval; μ is fixed and this interval either contains it or not.
items.source: Stanford Intro to Statistics, Module: Confidence intervals

items.title: One-sample t test decision
items.prompt: Test H₀: μ = 100 against Hₐ: μ ≠ 100 at α = 0.05. A sample of n = 16 gives x̄ = 104 and s = 10. Compute t and its degrees of freedom, then decide. (Critical value: t* = 2.131 for df = 15, two-sided 5%.)
items.answer:
SE = s/√n = 10/√16 = 10/4 = 2.5.
t = (104 − 100)/2.5 = 4/2.5 = 1.6, df = 16 − 1 = 15.
|t| = 1.6 < 2.131, so fail to reject H₀ at the 5% level (two-sided p ≈ 0.13).
Conclusion: the data do not give convincing evidence that μ differs from 100. That is not proof that μ = 100.
items.source: Stanford Intro to Statistics, Module: Tests of significance (t test)

items.title: What a p-value means
items.prompt:
A study reports p = 0.03 for H₀: "the new drug has no effect." Which statements are true?
(a) There is a 3% chance H₀ is true.
(b) If H₀ were true, results at least as extreme as these would occur about 3% of the time.
(c) At α = 0.05 we reject H₀; at α = 0.01 we do not.
(d) The drug has a large effect.
items.hint: A p-value is computed assuming H₀ is true. It says nothing about effect size.
items.answer:
True: (b) and (c).
(a) is false: the p-value is P(data this extreme | H₀), not P(H₀ | data).
(b) is the definition.
(c) is true because 0.03 ≤ 0.05 but 0.03 > 0.01.
(d) is false: a small p-value can come from a tiny effect measured with a large sample. Report a confidence interval to show size.
items.source: Stanford Intro to Statistics, Module: Tests of significance (p-values)

items.title: Standard error of the mean
items.prompt:
A population has mean μ = 100 and standard deviation σ = 15. You draw a random sample of n = 25.
(1) What are the mean and standard error of the sampling distribution of x̄?
(2) About how likely is x̄ > 106?
(3) What n would halve the standard error?
items.hint: SE = σ/√n. By the central limit theorem x̄ is roughly normal; standardize with z = (x̄ − μ)/SE.
items.source: Stanford Intro to Statistics, Module: Sampling distributions and the central limit theorem

items.title: Regression line from summary stats
items.prompt:
Hours studied (x) and exam score (y): x̄ = 5, sx = 2, ȳ = 70, sy = 10, correlation r = 0.6.
Find the least-squares line ŷ = a + b·x, predict the score for 7 hours, interpret the slope, and give the fraction of score variation the line explains.
items.hint: b = r·sy/sx. The line passes through (x̄, ȳ), so a = ȳ − b·x̄.
items.answer:
b = r·sy/sx = 0.6 × 10/2 = 3.
a = ȳ − b·x̄ = 70 − 3 × 5 = 55.
ŷ = 55 + 3x. At x = 7: ŷ = 55 + 21 = 76.
Slope: each extra hour studied is associated with a 3-point higher predicted score, on average. Association, not causation, since this is observational.
R² = r² = 0.36, so the line explains 36% of the variation in scores.
items.source: Stanford Intro to Statistics, Module: Regression

items.title: Bayes: positive test, rare disease
items.prompt: A disease affects 1% of people. A test is positive for 90% of people who have it and for 5% of people who do not. A random person tests positive. What is P(disease | positive)?
items.hint: P(D | +) = P(+ | D)P(D) / P(+). Get P(+) from both ways a positive can happen.
items.answer:
P(+ and D) = 0.90 × 0.01 = 0.009.
P(+ and not D) = 0.05 × 0.99 = 0.0495.
P(+) = 0.009 + 0.0495 = 0.0585.
P(D | +) = 0.009/0.0585 = 90/585 = 2/13 ≈ 0.154, about 15%.
Most positives are false positives because healthy people vastly outnumber sick ones.
items.source: Stanford Intro to Statistics, Module: Probability (Bayes' rule)

items.title: Sample size for a poll
items.prompt: How many people must a poll survey so that a 95% confidence interval for a proportion has a margin of error of at most 3 percentage points, with no prior guess for p?
items.hint: Margin = z*·√(p(1 − p)/n). With no guess, use p = 0.5, which maximizes p(1 − p).
items.source: Stanford Intro to Statistics, Module: Confidence intervals (proportions)

items.title: Var(x̄) = σ²/n
items.prompt: Let X₁, …, Xₙ be independent, each with mean μ and variance σ². Prove E(x̄) = μ and Var(x̄) = σ²/n, where x̄ = (X₁ + … + Xₙ)/n. Which step needs independence?
items.hint: Var(cY) = c²Var(Y). The variance of a sum equals the sum of the variances only when the covariances sum to zero (for example, independent variables).
items.answer:
E(x̄) = (1/n)·Σ E(Xᵢ) = (1/n)·nμ = μ, by linearity (no independence needed).
Var(x̄) = (1/n²)·Var(Σ Xᵢ).
Independence makes every Cov(Xᵢ, Xⱼ) = 0 for i ≠ j, so Var(Σ Xᵢ) = Σ Var(Xᵢ) = nσ².
So Var(x̄) = nσ²/n² = σ²/n, and SE = σ/√n. Independence is used only in the variance-of-a-sum step.
items.source: Stanford Intro to Statistics, Module: Sampling distributions

items.title: Expected matches (hat check)
items.prompt: n people check their hats, and the hats are handed back in a uniformly random order. What is the expected number of people who get their own hat back?
items.hint: Write the count as a sum of indicators and use linearity of expectation, which holds even for dependent terms.
items.answer:
Let Iᵢ = 1 if person i gets their own hat. The count is X = I₁ + … + Iₙ.
P(Iᵢ = 1) = 1/n (their hat is equally likely to be in any of the n positions), so E(Iᵢ) = 1/n.
By linearity, E(X) = n × 1/n = 1, for every n. The Iᵢ are dependent, but linearity does not care.
items.source: Harvard STAT 110 (Blitzstein & Hwang), Ch. 4: Expectation, indicator r.v.s

items.title: Birthday problem
items.prompt: In a room of 23 people with birthdays independent and uniform over 365 days (ignore leap years), what is the probability that at least two share a birthday?
items.hint: Compute the complement: everyone has a different birthday.
items.answer:
P(all different) = (365/365)(364/365)(363/365)…(343/365) = Π from k = 0 to 22 of (365 − k)/365 ≈ 0.4927.
P(at least one shared) = 1 − 0.4927 ≈ 0.5073, just over 50%.
Intuition: there are C(23, 2) = 253 pairs, each matching with probability 1/365.
items.source: Harvard STAT 110 (Blitzstein & Hwang), Ch. 1: Probability and counting

items.title: Expected rolls until a six
items.prompt: You roll a fair die until the first 6 appears. What is the expected number of rolls? Derive it by conditioning on the first roll.
items.hint: Let E be the answer. After a non-6 first roll, the process starts over.
items.answer:
With probability 1/6 the first roll is a 6 and we stop after 1 roll. With probability 5/6 we used 1 roll and start over.
E = 1 + (5/6)·E, so (1/6)·E = 1, and E = 6.
This matches the geometric mean 1/p with p = 1/6.
items.source: MIT 6.041SC (Bertsekas & Tsitsiklis), Ch. 2: Total expectation theorem

items.title: √2 is irrational
items.prompt: Prove that √2 is irrational.
items.hint: Assume √2 = p/q in lowest terms and show both p and q are even.
items.answer:
Suppose √2 = p/q with integers p, q, q ≠ 0, and gcd(p, q) = 1.
Squaring: p² = 2q², so p² is even. If p were odd, p² would be odd, so p is even: p = 2k.
Then 4k² = 2q², so q² = 2k² is even, and q is even too.
Both even contradicts gcd(p, q) = 1. So no such fraction exists and √2 is irrational.
items.source: Yale CS202 (Aspnes, Notes on Discrete Mathematics): Proof by contradiction

items.title: Pigeonhole: 5 points in a square
items.prompt: Prove that among any 5 points in a 1 × 1 square (boundary included), some two are at distance at most √2/2.
items.hint: Cut the square into 4 pieces. How far apart can two points in one piece be?
items.answer:
Split the square into 4 closed squares of side 1/2. Every point lies in at least one of them.
5 points, 4 small squares: by pigeonhole, some small square holds two of the points.
The farthest two points of a side-1/2 square can be is its diagonal: √((1/2)² + (1/2)²) = √(1/2) = √2/2.
So those two points are within √2/2 of each other.
items.source: Yale CS202 (Aspnes, Notes on Discrete Mathematics): Pigeonhole principle

items.title: Infinitely many primes
items.prompt: Prove that there are infinitely many primes.
items.hint: Given any finite list of primes, build a number none of them divides.
items.answer:
Suppose p₁, …, pₖ were all the primes. Let N = p₁·p₂·…·pₖ + 1.
N > 1, so N has some prime factor q.
Each pᵢ divides p₁·…·pₖ, so pᵢ leaves remainder 1 when dividing N; no pᵢ divides N.
So q is a prime not on the list, a contradiction. Hence there are infinitely many primes.
(N itself need not be prime; it only needs a prime factor outside the list.)
items.source: MIT 6.042J (Lehman, Leighton & Meyer, 2017 edition), Ch. 9: Number theory

items.title: Σ i = n(n+1)/2 by induction
items.prompt: Prove by induction that 1 + 2 + … + n = n(n + 1)/2 for every integer n ≥ 1.
items.hint: Base case n = 1. For the step, add n + 1 to both sides of P(n).
items.answer:
P(n): Σ from i = 1 to n of i = n(n + 1)/2.
Base: n = 1. Left side 1, right side 1·2/2 = 1. True.
Step: assume P(n). Then Σ from i = 1 to n + 1 of i = n(n + 1)/2 + (n + 1) = (n + 1)(n/2 + 1) = (n + 1)(n + 2)/2, which is P(n + 1).
By induction P(n) holds for all n ≥ 1.
items.source: MIT 6.042J (Lehman, Leighton & Meyer, 2017 edition), Ch. 5: Induction

items.title: 6 divides n³ − n
items.prompt: Prove that n³ − n is divisible by 6 for every integer n.
items.hint: Factor it.
items.answer:
n³ − n = n(n² − 1) = (n − 1)·n·(n + 1), a product of three consecutive integers.
Among any two consecutive integers one is even, so 2 divides the product.
Among any three consecutive integers one is a multiple of 3, so 3 divides the product.
Since gcd(2, 3) = 1, 2·3 = 6 divides it.
items.source: MIT 6.042J (Lehman, Leighton & Meyer, 2017 edition), Ch. 9: Divisibility

items.title: d/dx x² = 2x from the limit
items.prompt: Using only the limit definition of the derivative, prove that the derivative of f(x) = x² is 2x.
items.hint: f'(x) = lim as h → 0 of (f(x + h) − f(x))/h. Expand (x + h)².
items.answer:
f'(x) = lim as h → 0 of ((x + h)² − x²)/h
= lim as h → 0 of (x² + 2xh + h² − x²)/h
= lim as h → 0 of (2xh + h²)/h
= lim as h → 0 of (2x + h)   (cancelling h is fine because h ≠ 0 inside the limit)
= 2x.
items.source: MIT 18.01 Single Variable Calculus, Unit 1: Derivatives

items.title: Gradient and directional derivative
items.prompt: Let f(x, y) = x²y + y³. Find ∇f at (1, 2), and the rate of change of f at (1, 2) in the direction of the vector (3, 4).
items.hint: D_u f = ∇f · u, where u is a UNIT vector.
items.source: MIT 18.02 Multivariable Calculus, Part II: Partial derivatives and the gradient

items.title: AB invertible ⇒ A and B invertible
items.prompt: A and B are n × n matrices and AB is invertible. Prove that A and B are both invertible.
items.hint: Show B has only the zero vector in its nullspace. Then write A in terms of AB and B⁻¹.
items.answer:
B: if Bx = 0 then (AB)x = A(Bx) = 0. AB is invertible, so x = 0. So N(B) = {0}, and a square matrix with trivial nullspace is invertible.
A: A = (AB)B⁻¹, a product of two invertible matrices, so A is invertible with A⁻¹ = B(AB)⁻¹.
(Squareness matters: for non-square A, B, AB can be invertible while neither A nor B is.)
items.source: MIT 18.06 Linear Algebra (Strang), Ch. 2: Inverse matrices

items.title: Rank-nullity
items.prompt: State the rank-nullity theorem for an m × n matrix A and sketch why it holds using elimination. Then: a 3 × 5 matrix has rank 2. What is the dimension of its nullspace?
items.hint: Reduce A to its row echelon form R. Count pivot columns and free columns.
items.answer:
Statement: rank(A) + dim N(A) = n, the number of columns.
Why: elimination to R does not change the nullspace. R has r = rank(A) pivot columns and n − r free columns. Each free variable gives one special solution (set it to 1, the other free variables to 0, solve for the pivots). These n − r vectors are independent (each has a 1 in a free slot where the others have 0) and every nullspace vector is a combination of them, so dim N(A) = n − r.
Example: n = 5, rank 2, so dim N(A) = 5 − 2 = 3.
items.source: MIT 18.06 Linear Algebra (Strang), Ch. 3: The nullspace and rank

items.title: 1/n → 0 (ε-N)
items.prompt: Using the ε-N definition of a limit, prove that the sequence 1/n converges to 0.
items.hint: Given ε > 0, the Archimedean property gives an integer N > 1/ε.
items.answer:
Let ε > 0. By the Archimedean property choose an integer N > 1/ε, so 1/N < ε.
For every n ≥ N: |1/n − 0| = 1/n ≤ 1/N < ε.
So for every ε > 0 there is an N with |1/n − 0| < ε for all n ≥ N, which is the definition of 1/n → 0.
items.source: MIT 18.100A Real Analysis, Lecture: Sequences and limits
